metadata.name: Influenza (seasonal flu)
metadata.emergency_level: Usually routine — but can cause severe illness/pneumonia in high-risk groups
metadata.severity: Self-limiting in most; potentially severe in elderly, pregnant, chronic disease, immunocompromised

overview.short_description: An acute respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses, typically with abrupt high fever, myalgia, headache and prostration, more systemic than a common cold.
overview.detailed_description: Influenza A and B viruses cause seasonal epidemics. Illness ranges from mild to severe; most healthy adults recover in about a week, but influenza causes substantial morbidity and mortality in high-risk groups and can be complicated by pneumonia (primary viral or secondary bacterial). Diagnosis is usually clinical during known circulation; antivirals and vaccination are the specific interventions.
overview.pathophysiology: Virus infects respiratory epithelium, causing epithelial damage and a strong systemic cytokine response responsible for fever, myalgia and malaise. Epithelial injury and impaired mucociliary clearance predispose to secondary bacterial infection (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus).
overview.etiology: Influenza A (subtypes by H and N surface proteins) and influenza B; antigenic drift causes seasonal epidemics, antigenic shift (influenza A) can cause pandemics. Droplet/aerosol and contact transmission.
overview.natural_history: Abrupt onset; fever and systemic symptoms usually settle in 3-5 days; cough and malaise may persist 1-2 weeks. Complications more likely at extremes of age and with comorbidity.
overview.prognosis: Good in healthy adults; higher risk of severe disease/death in elderly, pregnant, young children, and those with chronic cardiac/respiratory/renal disease, diabetes, or immunosuppression.

prevalence.value: Seasonal epidemics affect an estimated 5-15% of the population annually (WHO).

incidence.value: Annual winter epidemics in temperate regions; year-round in tropics.

mortality.value: WHO estimates hundreds of thousands of respiratory deaths globally each year, concentrated in the elderly and high-risk groups.

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; severe disease at extremes of age.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; seasonal timing varies by hemisphere.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Crowding, close contact; not being vaccinated.
risk_factors.smoking: Increases risk of severe respiratory illness and complications.
risk_factors.alcohol: Excess associated with higher pneumonia risk.
risk_factors.obesity: Independent risk factor for severe influenza.
risk_factors.hypertension: Not a direct risk factor; comorbid cardiac disease increases risk.
risk_factors.pregnancy: Higher risk of severe disease and complications — a priority group for vaccination and antivirals.
risk_factors.occupation: Healthcare and frontline workers have higher exposure.
risk_factors.travel: Crowded travel and differing hemispheric seasons increase exposure.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Chronic cardiac, respiratory (asthma/COPD), renal, hepatic, neurological disease and immunosuppression increase risk.

chief_complaints.complaint: Sudden high fever and feeling very unwell

chief_complaints.importance: Prominent, helps distinguish from a cold

symptoms.importance: Key feature; abrupt onset distinguishes from cold
Prominent; more than in a cold
RED FLAG — suggests pneumonia or cardiac complication

negative_findings.finding: Gradual onset with only mild/low-grade fever
negative_findings.why_important: Argues against influenza and towards common cold

negative_findings.finding: No breathlessness, normal saturations, clear chest

history_questions.question: Was the onset sudden with high fever and body aches?
Is influenza circulating locally / any known contacts?
Do you have breathlessness, chest pain, or are you coughing up discoloured sputum/blood?
Are you pregnant, elderly, or do you have a chronic illness or weakened immunity?
history_questions.why_ask: Identifies high-risk groups needing antivirals and closer review

history_questions.question: Have you had the flu vaccine this season?
history_questions.why_ask: Affects probability and future prevention advice

physical_examination.examination: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, chest auscultation
physical_examination.expected_finding: Usually clear; focal signs/hypoxia suggest pneumonia

vital_signs.blood_pressure: Usually normal; low BP suggests sepsis/severe disease
vital_signs.respiratory_rate: Raised RR is a red flag for pneumonia
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: >=95% expected; hypoxia is a red flag

laboratory_tests.indication: Hospitalised, high-risk, or when it changes management/infection control
laboratory_tests.diagnostic_value: Confirms diagnosis; not needed for typical outpatient cases in season

laboratory_tests.test_name: FBC, CRP, U&E, chest imaging (if complicated)

imaging.when_needed: Suspected pneumonia (focal signs, hypoxia, severe illness)
imaging.expected_findings: Infiltrates if complicated; normal in uncomplicated influenza

ecg.findings: May show myocarditis-related changes in rare complications.

other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Sputum/blood cultures if secondary bacterial infection/sepsis suspected
other_diagnostic_tests.pcr: Respiratory viral PCR panel (including influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2) where indicated

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical: acute onset of fever plus respiratory symptoms (cough/sore throat) with systemic features (myalgia, headache, malaise) during influenza circulation — 'influenza-like illness (ILI)'. Laboratory confirmation by PCR/antigen when required.
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: ILI case definitions (e.g., fever + cough) used for surveillance; CRB-65/CURB-65 assess pneumonia severity if complicated.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Gradual onset, low-grade/no fever, less systemic

differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Loss of smell/taste or known COVID contact?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Focal chest signs, breathlessness, hypoxia, pleuritic pain
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are you breathless or coughing up discoloured sputum?

differential_diagnosis.disease: Other systemic infection (e.g., early sepsis, malaria if travel, dengue)
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any recent travel to endemic areas?

diagnostic_questions.question: Did your illness start abruptly with high fever and severe body aches?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Abrupt high fever + myalgia favours influenza

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you breathless or is your oxygen level low?

next_best_question.question: Are you in a high-risk group (pregnant, elderly, chronic illness, immunocompromised) and how breathless are you?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Low-risk, well -> symptomatic care + safety-net; high-risk or breathless -> consider antivirals and assess for complications/admission

red_flags.finding: Breathlessness, rapid breathing, or oxygen saturation <95%
red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent assessment for pneumonia; consider admission

red_flags.finding: Confusion, marked lethargy, low blood pressure, or signs of sepsis
Chest pain or symptoms of myocarditis
High-risk patient (pregnant, elderly, chronic disease, immunocompromised) with worsening symptoms
red_flags.immediate_action: Early antiviral consideration and close review/admission

red_flags.finding: Deterioration after initial improvement (secondary bacterial infection)
red_flags.immediate_action: Reassess for bacterial pneumonia; consider antibiotics

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected pneumonia or severe/complicated influenza; high-risk patient deteriorating.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Respiratory failure/hypoxia, sepsis, myocarditis, or seriously unwell high-risk patient.

late: Rarely myocarditis, encephalitis, or Guillain-Barré syndrome

initial_management.supportive_care: Rest, fluids, antipyretics/analgesia; safety-net advice; isolate to reduce spread.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Oseltamivir; Zanamivir; Paracetamol; NSAID. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: CDC_FLU_2026.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Rest and hydration; stay off work/school while febrile; hand and respiratory hygiene.
initial_management.follow_up: Return/seek help if breathless, not improving after ~1 week, or deteriorating; proactive review of high-risk patients.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen). Antiviral neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir/zanamivir) are recommended for high-risk patients and severe/hospitalised cases, ideally started within 48 hours of onset; consider per local guidance during circulation. Antibiotics ONLY if secondary bacterial infection is suspected.

patient_education.home_advice: Flu usually comes on suddenly with fever, aches and tiredness and gets better in about a week. Rest, drink fluids, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen. Stay home to avoid spreading it. Get urgent help if you become breathless, have chest pain, cough up blood, become confused, or if you are in a high-risk group and getting worse.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: الإنفلونزا تبدأ عادةً فجأةً بحرارة وآلام وإرهاق وتتحسّن خلال أسبوع تقريباً. ارتَح واشرب السوائل وتناول الباراسيتامول أو الإيبوبروفين، والزم المنزل لتجنّب نقل العدوى. اطلب المساعدة العاجلة إذا صرت تلهث، أو شعرت بألم في الصدر، أو خرج دم مع السعال، أو حدث تشوّش، أو كنت من الفئات عالية الخطورة وتزداد سوءاً.
patient_education.prevention: Annual influenza vaccination (especially high-risk groups), hand hygiene, staying home when unwell.
patient_education.warning_signs: Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, confusion, persistent high fever, or deterioration after initial improvement.

prevention.vaccination: Annual influenza vaccine is the primary prevention; recommended for elderly, pregnant, young children, chronic disease, immunocompromised, and healthcare workers.
prevention.lifestyle: Hand and respiratory hygiene; avoiding contact when unwell.
prevention.screening: Not applicable; surveillance monitors circulating strains.

evidence.evidence_level: High for vaccination benefit; moderate for antiviral benefit (greatest in high-risk/early treatment).
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by CDC_FLU_2026; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
